Situation Report Lebanon Crisis 23 June - 7 July 2026 
 
Highlights 
The humanitarian situation in Lebanon remains fragile despite a reduction in hostilities, with significant and persistent humanitarian, protection, and early recovery needs. Daily airstrikes and military operations, particularly in southern Lebanon, continue to pose risks to civilians and limit safe returns, highlighting the potential for renewed escalation despite ongoing diplomatic efforts. Since 2 March 2026, a reported 4,304 people have been killed and 12,203 have been injured. 
Women and girls are bearing the brunt of the crisis, facing heightened protection and gender-based violence (GBV) risks, disrupted health services, including for maternal health, and reduced access to safe and dignified support. 
Since the onset of the crisis, UNFPA has reached over 150,000 displaced people with sexual and reproductive health (SRH) and GBV services. These services have been delivered through support to 55 health facilities, nine mobile medical units, 24 mobile GBV teams, and 19 women and girls’ safe spaces (WGSSs), serving collective shelters and host communities.

UNFPA Situation Report I Lebanon I 23 June - 7 July 2026 
Situation Overview 
An estimated 646,107 people in Lebanon have begun returning to their areas of origin, with population movements increasing by 23 per cent in the past two weeks. The largest share of returnees 
has
 
been
 
reported
 
in
 
South
 
and
 
Nabatieh
 
governorates,
 
where
 
the
 
conflict
 
has
 
caused
 
extensive
 
damage
 
to
 
housing,
 
infrastructure,
 
and
 
essential
 
services.
 
Despite
 
the
 
increase
 
in
 
returns,
 
movements
 
remain
 
cautious
 
and
 
uneven.
 
Many
 
households
 
continue
 
to
 
undertake
 
temporary
 
“go-and-see”
 
visits
 
to
 
assess
 
levels
 
of
 
destruction,
 
security
 
conditions,
 
and
 
service
 
availability
 
before
 
returning
 
permanently.
 
Displacement levels continue to decline, with the proportion of displaced persons residing in 
collective
 
shelters
 
decreasing
 
from
 
11
 
per
 
cent
 
to
 
9
 
per
 
cent
 
over
 
the
 
past
 
two
 
weeks.
 
The
 
number
 
of
 registered collective sites has reduced from over 600 to 430 and the collective-site population has reduced to less than half from over 100,000 to 47,143 individuals since 25 June. As of 1 July 2026, some 499,784 internally displaced persons have been recorded across Lebanon. New shelters are being established in Nabatieh and South governorates to accommodate individuals undertaking 
"go-and-see"
 
visits
 
prior
 
to
 
return,
 
as
 
well
 
as
 
households
 
whose
 
homes
 
have
 
been
 
damaged,
 
destroyed,
 
or
 
remain
 
inaccessible.
 
Many
 
displaced
 
households
 
continue
 
to
 
face
 
uncertainty
 
regarding
 
future
 
accommodation
 
arrangements,
 
including
 
a
 
need
 
for
 
secondary
 
shelter
 
solutions
 
and
 
cash
 
support
 
for
 
rent.
 
Women and girls in collective shelters, temporary accommodation, and return areas continue to face 
protection
 
risks.
 
Despite
 
reduced
 
shelter
 
occupancy,
 
key
 
vulnerabilities
 
persist,
 
including
 
limited
 
privacy,
 
unsafe
 
or
 
inadequately
 
segregated
 
water
 
and
 
sanitation
 
facilities,
 
weak
 
access
 
to
 
confidential
 
GBV
 
services,
 
and
 
rising
 
rental
 
costs
 
and
 
eviction
 
threats.
 
Female-headed
 
households,
 
adolescent
 
girls,
 
pregnant
 
and
 
lactating
 
women,
 
older
 
persons,
 
and
 
persons
 
with
 
disabilities
 
encounter
 
specific
 
barriers
 
to
 
safety
 
and
 
services.
 
Sustained
 
outreach,
 
survivor-centred
 
GBV
 
response,
 
functional
 
referral
 
pathways,
 
and
 
risk
 
mitigation
 
measures
 
are
 
essential
 
across
 
shelters
 
and
 
communities
 
hosting
 
displaced
 
and
 
returning
 
families.
 
Health services remain severely strained. Three hospitals and 36 primary health centres (PHCs) remain closed, while 17 hospitals are damaged. Although some hospitals in southern Lebanon have resumed essential maternity services, access to safe maternal and newborn care remains limited, 
particularly
 
in
 
Bent
 
Jbeil
 
and
 
Nabatieh
 
districts,
 
where
 
maternity
 
services
 
have
 
not
 
been
 
fully
 
restored
 
and
 
emergency
 
care
 
has
 
been
 
prioritized.
 
Returns
 
to
 
areas
 
with
 
widespread
 
damage,
 
insecurity,
 
and
 
limited
 
services
 
are
 
further
 
disrupting
 
service
 
provision,
 
mobile
 
service
 
deployment,
 
and
 
continuity
 
of
 
care.
 
Sustained
 
support
 
for
 
primary
 
healthcare,
 
mobile
 
outreach,
 
obstetric
 
and
 
newborn
 
care,
 
and
 
GBV
 
services
 
is
 
essential,
 
particularly
 
in
 
southern
 
Lebanon,
 
Saida,
 
Beirut,
 
and
 
Mount
 
Lebanon.
 
 
UNFPA estimates that 390,000 women of childbearing age are among the displaced and returnee 
population,
 
of
 
whom
 
approximately
 
16,000
 
are
 
pregnant,
 
and
 
around
 
1,800
 
women
 
are
 
expected
 
to
 
give
 
birth
 
every
 
month.
 
Pregnant
 
women
 
are
 
returning
 
to
 
areas
 
with
 
significant
 
damage
 
to
 
health
 
infrastructure,
 
in
 
particular
 
for
 
maternal
 
healthcare,
 
underscoring
 
the
 
continued
 
need
 
for
 
life-saving
 
SRH
 
supplies
 
and
 
services.
 
The operating environment remains challenging. Access constraints and funding shortfalls continue to 
limit
 
the
 
response.
 
Damage
 
to
 
infrastructure
 
and
 
service
 
networks,
 
together
 
with
 
persisting
 
insecurity
 
in
 
parts
 
of
 
South
 
and
 
Nabatieh
 
governorates,
 
continue
 
to
 
affect
 
humanitarian
 
operations
 
and
 
early
 
recovery
 
efforts.

Funding Status 
UNFPA launched a revised Flash Appeal in June, aligned with the revised Inter-Agency Lebanon Flash Appeal appealing for US $25 million to meet the urgent needs of 
450,000
 
people
 
from
 
March
 
to
 
August
 
2026.
 
To
 
date,
 
only
 
16
 
per
 
cent
 
of
 
the
 
required
 
funding
 
has
 
been
 
secured.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
"When hospitals close and healthcare collapses, it is 
pregnant
 
women
 
who
 
pay
 
the
 
price
 
because
 
women
 
do
 
not
 
stop
 
giving
 
birth
 
in

midst
 
of
 
a
 
conflict.
 
No
 
woman
 
should
 
have
 
to
 
risk
 
her
 
life
 
—
 
or
 
her
 
baby's
 
life
 
—
 
to
 
give
 
birth.
 
Women’s
 
and
 
girls’
 
health
 
and
 
rights
 
are
 
non-negotiable
 
even
 
in
 
a
 
crisis."
 
 
— Anandita Philipose, UNFPA Representative in Lebanon.

Article 5 / A Member of the United Nations against which preventive or enforcement action has been taken by the Security Council may be suspended from the exercise of the rights and privileges of mem- bership by the General Assembly upon the recom- mendation of the Security Council.

Article 6 A Member of the United Nations which has persistently violated the Principles contained in the present Charter may be expelled from the Organization by the General Assembly upon the recommendation of the Security Council.

Accordingly, our respective Governments, through representatives assembled in the city of San Francisco, who have exhibited their full powers found to be in good and due form, have agreed to the present Charter of the United Nations and do hereby establish an international organization to be known as the United Nations.

related.excerpt: Nearly 100 US service members have been injured over the last two weeks of escalating strikes on Iran, the Pentagon has said, as Tehran launched a wave of reprisals to the tenth consecutive night of attacks. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Tuesday they had targeted US military sites including air defence systems and a radar installation in Bahrain and Kuwait, while a tanker in the strait of Hormuz reported being ⁠struck by an unknown projectile, forcing its crew to abandon the vessel and board a lifeboat. Kuwait, Bahrain and Jordan all said they had activated defences to repel the attacks, but the scale of US injuries at facilities across the region over recent week is likely to bring greater scrutiny to Iran’s reprisal attacks. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said the vast majority of those injured only experienced “minor concussions” and 96% had since returned to work. Parnell was responding to a New York Times report that the Pentagon has withheld information about troop injuries from Iranian strikes. He denied that the Pentagon was hiding data about injuries.
